meta.description: Yes — it’s genuinely William James, from the closing of his 1895 essay “Is Life Worth Living?” The fuller line begins “Be not afraid of life.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Believe that life is worth living and your belief will help create the fact'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely William James — the closing words of his 1895 essay “Is Life Worth Living?”, later collected in The Will to Believe (1897).

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing words of James’s essay “Is Life Worth Living?” — delivered as an address in May 1895 and published in the International Journal of Ethics that October, then collected in The Will to Believe and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy (1897). The full sentence is preceded by “Be not afraid of life.”

source.excerpt: These, then, are my last words to you: Be not afraid of life. Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact. The ‘scientific proof’ that you are right may not be clear before the day of judgment … is reached.

author.name: William James
author.heading: About William James
author.metaLine: 1842–1910 · American philosopher & psychologist, a founder of pragmatism
author.bio: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist, often called the father of American psychology and a leading figure in the pragmatist tradition. His major works include The Principles of Psychology (1890), The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), and the essay collection The Will to Believe (1897), in which “Is Life Worth Living?” appears. The idea that belief can be self-fulfilling — that conviction helps bring about the very fact it affirms — is central to his philosophy of the “will to believe.”

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — but usually cut short
misattribution.intro: This one is the exception among “famous name” quotes: it really is William James, word for word. What circulates is not a false attribution but a truncation.

items.why: The quotation almost always appears as the bare middle sentence, stripped of its source. In the essay it is the second of three sentences: “Be not afraid of life. Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact” — see the primary text.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is authentically James’s, from the close of “Is Life Worth Living?” (1895); the only distortion is dropping the opening line “Be not afraid of life,” as Quote Investigator documents.

context.heading: Belief as a self-fulfilling act
lead: James delivered “Is Life Worth Living?” to the Harvard YMCA in 1895, arguing against the pessimism and suicidal despair he saw around him. His answer was neither blind optimism nor proof, but a wager: in some matters, believing that a thing is so helps make it so.

The closing exhortation gathers that argument into a single command. Conviction, for James, is not a passive report on reality but a force that can help bring the hoped-for reality into being — the heart of his “will to believe.”
